item.title: Classifying Alloys of Copper, Silver, and Iron by Atomic Radius
item.stimulus:
Approximate atomic radii of five elements are listed below.

Element | Atomic radius (pm)
Cu | 128
Ni | 124
Ag | 144
Fe | 126
N | 71

Cupronickel, used in some coins, is an alloy of copper and nickel. Nitrided iron is an alloy of iron that contains a small amount of nitrogen. Sterling silver is an alloy of silver and copper. Answer the following.

parts.prompt: Describe a particle-level model of pure solid copper that shows the essential features of metallic bonding.

criteria.text: Describes an array of positive copper ions surrounded by delocalized valence electrons (a sea of electrons) that are not associated with any single ion.
criteria.evidence: Response states that solid copper consists of copper cations arranged in a regular array and that the valence electrons are delocalized throughout the solid rather than bound to individual atoms.
criteria.fix: Describe two features: copper cations held in a regular array, and valence electrons spread through the whole solid rather than belonging to one atom.

parts.prompt: Classify cupronickel as a substitutional alloy or an interstitial alloy, and describe where the nickel atoms are located. Justify your answer using the data.

criteria.text: Classifies cupronickel as a substitutional alloy in which nickel atoms take the place of copper atoms at positions in the lattice, because Cu (128 pm) and Ni (124 pm) have comparable radii.
criteria.evidence: Response states substitutional, says that Ni atoms replace (substitute for) Cu atoms in the lattice, and supports this by noting that the two radii are similar.
criteria.fix: Compare the two radii; atoms of similar size can replace one another at lattice positions, which defines a substitutional alloy.

parts.prompt: Classify nitrided iron as a substitutional alloy or an interstitial alloy, and describe where the nitrogen atoms are located. Justify your answer using the data.

criteria.text: Classifies nitrided iron as an interstitial alloy in which nitrogen atoms occupy the spaces between iron atoms, because N (71 pm) is much smaller than Fe (126 pm).
criteria.evidence: Response states interstitial, says the N atoms fill spaces (interstices) between Fe atoms in the lattice, and supports this by noting that the N radius is much smaller than the Fe radius.
criteria.fix: When one atom is much smaller, it fits into the gaps between the larger atoms; name this an interstitial alloy and cite the radii.

parts.prompt: A student claims that sterling silver must be an interstitial alloy because copper atoms are smaller than silver atoms. Evaluate the student's claim using the data.

criteria.text: States that the claim is incorrect: Cu (128 pm) is only slightly smaller than Ag (144 pm), so the radii are comparable and copper substitutes for silver, making sterling silver a substitutional alloy; interstitial alloys require a much smaller atom, as with N (71 pm) in Fe (126 pm).
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim and explains that the Ag and Cu radii are comparable (differing by only about 11%), so sterling silver is substitutional; being merely smaller is not enough for an interstitial alloy.
criteria.fix: Judge how large the size difference is, not just which atom is smaller; only a much smaller atom fits between atoms of the host metal.

item.model_answer:
(a) Solid copper is a regular three-dimensional array of positive copper ions. The valence electrons are not attached to any one ion; they are delocalized and move freely throughout the whole solid as a sea of electrons that holds the cations together.

(b) Cupronickel is a substitutional alloy. The radii of Cu (128 pm) and Ni (124 pm) are very similar, so nickel atoms can take the place of copper atoms at positions in the copper lattice.

(c) Nitrided iron is an interstitial alloy. A nitrogen atom (71 pm) is much smaller than an iron atom (126 pm), so the nitrogen atoms fit into the spaces between the iron atoms while the iron atoms keep their lattice positions.

(d) The claim is incorrect. Copper atoms (128 pm) are only about 11% smaller than silver atoms (144 pm), so the radii are comparable. Copper atoms therefore replace silver atoms at lattice positions, and sterling silver is a substitutional alloy. An interstitial alloy forms only when one atom is much smaller than the other, as with N (71 pm) in Fe (126 pm).
item.verification_python:
r={'Cu':128,'Ni':124,'Ag':144,'Fe':126,'N':71}
assert abs(r['Ni']/r['Cu']-1)<0.05
assert r['N']/r['Fe']<0.6
diff=(r['Ag']-r['Cu'])/r['Ag']
assert abs(diff-0.11)<0.005
assert r['Cu']<r['Ag']
assert r['Cu']/r['Ag']>0.85
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Atom Ratios and Structure Types in Steel and Cupronickel
item.stimulus:
A metallurgy student studies two alloys and pure nickel.

Alloy 1 is a carbon steel. Analysis of a 100.00 g sample shows that it contains 0.90 g of carbon and 99.10 g of iron, with no other elements present.

Alloy 2 is cupronickel, a coin metal made of copper and nickel atoms mixed throughout the solid.

The student looks up the following atomic radii.

Element | Atomic radius (pm)
Fe | 126
C | 77
Cu | 128
Ni | 124

Molar masses: C = 12.01 g/mol, Fe = 55.85 g/mol.
item.model_answer:
(a) Moles of C = 0.90 g ÷ 12.01 g/mol = 0.0749 mol. Moles of Fe = 99.10 g ÷ 55.85 g/mol = 1.774 mol. The ratio of C atoms to Fe atoms is 0.0749 ÷ 1.774 = 0.0422 C atoms per Fe atom. Scaling to 100 Fe atoms gives 0.0422 × 100 = 4.2 C atoms per 100 Fe atoms. The answer has 2 significant figures because the mass of carbon, 0.90 g, has 2 significant figures.

(b) Alloy 1 is an interstitial alloy. The carbon atom (77 pm) is much smaller than the iron atom (126 pm), only about 61% of its radius. The small C atoms therefore fit into the empty spaces (interstices) between the Fe atoms in the iron lattice instead of replacing Fe atoms.

(c) Alloy 2 is a substitutional alloy. Copper (128 pm) and nickel (124 pm) have comparable radii, differing by only about 3%. A Ni atom can therefore take the place of a Cu atom at a lattice position without greatly disturbing the lattice.

(d) Solid nickel consists of positive Ni ions (cations) arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional array. The valence electrons are delocalized: they are not tied to any one nucleus and move freely throughout the whole solid, forming a sea of electrons. The Coulombic attraction between the positive Ni ions and the surrounding delocalized electrons holds the metal together.
item.verification_python:
import math
mC = 0.90
mFe = 99.10
MC = 12.01
MFe = 55.85
nC = mC / MC
nFe = mFe / MFe
assert abs(nC - 0.0749) < 0.0001
assert abs(nFe - 1.774) < 0.001
ratio = nC / nFe
assert abs(ratio - 0.0422) < 0.0001
per100 = ratio * 100
assert round(per100, 1) == 4.2
assert abs(round(ratio, 3) - 0.042) < 1e-9
assert abs(mC + mFe - 100.00) < 1e-9
frac = 77 / 126
assert abs(frac - 0.61) < 0.01
diff = (128 - 124) / 128
assert abs(diff - 0.03) < 0.005
assert 128 - 124 == 4
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

criteria.evidence: Converts 0.90 g C to about 0.0749 mol and 99.10 g Fe to about 1.774 mol. Takes the mole (atom) ratio and scales it to 100 Fe atoms, giving 4.2 reported to 2 significant figures.
criteria.fix: Convert each element's mass to moles using its molar mass, divide the moles, then round to the fewest significant figures in the data.

criteria.text: Identifies cupronickel as a substitutional alloy because Cu (128 pm) and Ni (124 pm) have comparable radii, so Ni atoms replace Cu atoms at lattice positions.
criteria.evidence: States substitutional. Notes that the Cu and Ni radii are similar (differ by only about 4 pm, about 3%). States that one kind of atom takes the place of the other in the lattice.
criteria.fix: When two metal atoms have nearly equal radii, explain that one atom replaces the other at lattice sites, which makes the alloy substitutional.

criteria.text: Describes solid nickel as an orderly array of positive Ni ions surrounded by delocalized valence electrons (a sea of electrons), held together by attraction between the cations and the electrons.
criteria.evidence: Identifies positive nickel ions (cations) arranged in a regular array. States that the valence electrons are delocalized, meaning they are not tied to individual atoms and move throughout the solid. States that the attraction between the positive ions and the delocalized electrons holds the solid together.
criteria.fix: Name both components of metallic bonding: positive metal ions in a lattice and mobile shared valence electrons, plus the attraction between them.

item.title: Metallic Bonding and Classifying Brass and Steel Alloys
item.stimulus:
Copper and iron are metals. Each is also the main component of a common alloy. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Carbon steel is an alloy of iron and carbon. The table lists approximate atomic radii and molar masses for the four elements.

Element | Atomic radius (pm) | Molar mass (g/mol)
Cu | 128 | 63.55
Zn | 134 | 65.38
Fe | 126 | 55.85
C | 77 | 12.01

A 1.000 kg sample of a carbon steel contains 4.0 g of carbon. The remaining 996.0 g is iron.
item.model_answer:
(a) Solid copper consists of a regular array of positive copper ions at the lattice positions. The valence electrons are not tied to any single atom; they are delocalized throughout the solid as a sea of electrons. The solid is held together by the attraction between the positive Cu ions and this sea of delocalized electrons.

(b) Brass is a substitutional alloy. The atomic radius of Cu (128 pm) is comparable to that of Zn (134 pm). Because the two atoms are similar in size, Zn atoms can replace Cu atoms at lattice positions.

(c) Carbon steel is an interstitial alloy. Iron atoms occupy the main lattice positions. A carbon atom (77 pm) is much smaller than an iron atom (126 pm), so the C atoms fit into the interstitial spaces between the Fe atoms instead of replacing them.

(d) Moles of Fe = 996.0 g ÷ 55.85 g/mol = 17.83 mol.
Moles of C = 4.0 g ÷ 12.01 g/mol = 0.333 mol.
Fe atoms per C atom = 17.83 mol ÷ 0.333 mol = 53.5.
Limited by the 2 significant figures in 4.0 g, the answer is about 54 Fe atoms per C atom.
item.verification_python:
import math
m_fe=996.0; m_c=4.0
M_fe=55.85; M_c=12.01
n_fe=m_fe/M_fe; n_c=m_c/M_c
assert abs(n_fe-17.83)<0.01
assert abs(n_c-0.333)<0.001
ratio=n_fe/n_c
assert abs(ratio-53.5)<0.1
assert round(ratio)==54
assert abs(1000.0-(m_fe+m_c))<1e-9
r={'Cu':128,'Zn':134,'Fe':126,'C':77}
assert abs(r['Zn']-r['Cu'])/r['Cu']<0.15
assert (r['Fe']-r['C'])/r['Fe']>0.3
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: Using the model of metallic bonding, describe the particles that occupy the lattice positions in solid copper and the interaction that holds the solid together.

criteria.text: Describes solid copper as an array of positive copper ions (cations) surrounded by delocalized valence electrons (a sea of electrons), with the attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons holding the solid together.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies positive Cu ions at the lattice positions, states that the valence electrons are delocalized or not bound to individual atoms, and names the attraction between the cations and those electrons as the bonding.
criteria.fix: Describe metallic bonding as positive metal ions in a fixed array attracted to valence electrons that are delocalized throughout the whole solid.
accepted_variants: Cu⁺ or Cu²⁺ cations in a lattice

parts.prompt: Classify brass as an interstitial alloy or a substitutional alloy. Justify your answer using data from the table.

criteria.text: Classifies brass as a substitutional alloy, because Cu (128 pm) and Zn (134 pm) have comparable radii, so Zn atoms can replace Cu atoms at lattice positions.
criteria.evidence: Response states substitutional and cites the similar radii of Cu and Zn, using the table values or an explicit comparison, as the reason Zn atoms take the place of Cu atoms in the lattice.
criteria.fix: Compare the two atomic radii: similar sizes mean one atom replaces the other at lattice sites, which makes the alloy substitutional.

parts.prompt: Classify carbon steel as an interstitial alloy or a substitutional alloy. Identify which type of atom occupies the main lattice positions, and justify your answer using data from the table.

criteria.text: Classifies carbon steel as an interstitial alloy. Fe atoms occupy the main lattice positions, and the much smaller C atoms (77 pm compared with 126 pm) fill the interstitial spaces between the Fe atoms.
criteria.evidence: Response states interstitial, identifies iron as the atom at the lattice positions, and justifies the classification by citing the significantly smaller radius of carbon, so that C fits in the spaces between Fe atoms.
criteria.fix: When one atom is much smaller than the host metal atom, state that it fills the gaps between host atoms, which makes the alloy interstitial.
accepted_variants: C occupies the interstices in the Fe lattice

parts.prompt: For the 1.000 kg steel sample described above, calculate the number of iron atoms present for each carbon atom. Report your answer to the correct number of significant figures.

criteria.text: Calculates about 54 Fe atoms per C atom: 996.0 g ÷ 55.85 g/mol = 17.83 mol Fe and 4.0 g ÷ 12.01 g/mol = 0.33 mol C, giving 17.83 ÷ 0.333 = 54, reported to 2 significant figures.
criteria.evidence: Response converts both masses to moles using the molar masses, takes the ratio of moles of Fe to moles of C, and reports about 54 with two significant figures. The value 53.5 is accepted only if the work is shown.
criteria.fix: Convert each mass to moles with its molar mass, then divide moles Fe by moles C; let the 2 significant figures of 4.0 g limit the answer.

item.title: Steel and Brass: Classifying Alloys and Their Structure
item.stimulus:
Two common alloys are steel, made mostly of iron with a small amount of carbon, and brass, made of copper and zinc. A student looks up the atomic radii and molar masses of the elements in these alloys. The values are listed in the table below.

Element | Atomic radius (pm) | Molar mass (g/mol)
Fe | 126 | 55.85
C | 77 | 12.01
Cu | 128 | 63.55
Zn | 134 | 65.38

The student prepares a brass sample by melting together 19.06 g of Cu and 6.54 g of Zn and letting the mixture cool into a uniform solid.
item.model_answer:
(a) Steel is an interstitial alloy. A C atom (77 pm) is much smaller than an Fe atom (126 pm); its radius is only about 61% of the Fe radius. The small C atoms therefore fit into the spaces (interstices) between the larger Fe atoms in the iron lattice instead of replacing Fe atoms.

(b) Brass is a substitutional alloy. Cu (128 pm) and Zn (134 pm) have comparable radii, differing by only about 5%. A Zn atom is too large to fit between Cu atoms, but it is similar enough in size to take the place of a Cu atom at a lattice site.

(c) moles Zn = 6.54 g ÷ 65.38 g/mol = 0.1000 mol
moles Cu = 19.06 g ÷ 63.55 g/mol = 0.2999 mol
total moles of atoms = 0.1000 + 0.2999 = 0.3999 mol
fraction of sites occupied by Zn = 0.1000 ÷ 0.3999 = 0.250 (three significant figures, limited by 6.54 g)

(d) The lattice sites in brass are occupied by positive metal ions, both Cu cations and Zn cations, with Zn ions substituting for some Cu ions. The valence electrons from all the atoms are delocalized and move freely throughout the solid as a sea of electrons rather than belonging to any one atom. The electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the surrounding delocalized electrons holds the solid together (metallic bonding).
item.verification_python:
import math
r_Fe, r_C, r_Cu, r_Zn = 126, 77, 128, 134
ratio_steel = r_C / r_Fe
assert abs(ratio_steel - 0.611) < 0.001
ratio_brass = r_Zn / r_Cu
assert abs((ratio_brass - 1) * 100 - 4.7) < 0.1
n_Zn = 6.54 / 65.38
n_Cu = 19.06 / 63.55
assert abs(n_Zn - 0.1000) < 0.00005
assert abs(n_Cu - 0.2999) < 0.00005
total = n_Zn + n_Cu
assert abs(total - 0.3999) < 0.00005
frac = n_Zn / total
assert abs(frac - 0.250) < 0.0005
assert round(frac, 3) == 0.250
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: Classify steel as an interstitial alloy or a substitutional alloy. Justify your answer using the atomic radii in the table.

criteria.text: Classifies steel as an interstitial alloy, justified by C (77 pm) being significantly smaller than Fe (126 pm), so C atoms fit in the spaces between Fe atoms.
criteria.evidence: Response states interstitial and compares the radii, noting C is much smaller than Fe (about 61% of its radius), so C occupies interstices in the Fe lattice.
criteria.fix: Compare the two radii: a much smaller atom fits in the gaps between larger atoms, which defines an interstitial alloy.

parts.prompt: Classify brass as an interstitial alloy or a substitutional alloy. Justify your answer using the atomic radii in the table.

criteria.text: Classifies brass as a substitutional alloy, justified by Cu (128 pm) and Zn (134 pm) having comparable radii, so Zn atoms replace Cu atoms at lattice sites.
criteria.evidence: Response states substitutional and notes the radii are similar (differ by about 5%), so Zn substitutes for Cu in the lattice rather than fitting between atoms.
criteria.fix: When two atoms have similar radii, one replaces the other at lattice sites; state that and cite both radii as evidence.

parts.prompt: Assume every Cu and Zn atom in the student's brass sample occupies a lattice site. Calculate the fraction of the lattice sites in the sample that are occupied by Zn atoms. Show your work and report your answer to the correct number of significant figures.

criteria.text: Calculates the fraction of lattice sites occupied by Zn as 0.250, using moles Zn = 6.54/65.38 = 0.1000 mol and moles Cu = 19.06/63.55 = 0.2999 mol.
criteria.evidence: Response converts both masses to moles, divides moles of Zn by total moles of metal atoms, and reports 0.250 (three significant figures).
criteria.fix: Convert each mass to moles with n = m/M, then divide moles of Zn by total moles of atoms; keep three significant figures.

parts.prompt: Describe the particle-level model of the bonding in the brass sample. Identify the particles located at the lattice sites and explain what holds them together.

criteria.text: Describes brass as an array of positive Cu and Zn ions (cations) surrounded by a sea of delocalized valence electrons, held together by attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies positive metal ions (both Cu and Zn) at lattice sites, states the valence electrons are delocalized (not bound to one atom), and names the cation-electron attraction as the bonding.
criteria.fix: State three things: positive metal ions at lattice sites, delocalized valence electrons shared by all ions, and attraction between them as the bond.
accepted_variants: metallic bonding with delocalized valence electrons
